extracted.intended_audience: members of Parliament and the educated British public (late 18th century); readers of political speeches and commentary
extracted.subtask_description: A transcribed/abstracted speech delivered in the House of Commons (1790) addressing the army estimates and a broad political critique of the French Revolution, its example, and implications for British policy. The material mixes argumentation about foreign policy, military organization, and principles of reform versus revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional confidence in ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence might become a vice, and jealousy a virtue, according to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess trust in ministers by whether their proposed measures (e.g., increases in peace establishments) conform with objective facts such as the true state of the European balance of power; do not grant blind confidence when independent indicators do not support ministerial claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of balance-of-power evidence to justify military size
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of a larger or smaller annual army depends upon the true state of the balance of power in Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An increase in peace establishments should be supported by a manifest appearance of necessity in the continental balance; lacking such evidence, Parliament ought to be skeptical and entertain jealousy rather than unqualified trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate foreign states by strength, not government form
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to her strength, not to her form of government, which we are to attend; republics, as well as monarchies, are susceptible of ambition, jealousy, and anger, the usual causes of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-policy judgment should focus on material capability and probable behavior rather than ideological labels; both republics and monarchies can threaten national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expanding military expenditure while rivals are temporarily weak
rubrics_metrics.description: If, while France continued in this swoon, we should go on increasing our expenses, we should certainly make ourselves less a match for her when it became our concern to arm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain restraint in building permanent advantages during a rival's temporary collapse to preserve long-term parity when they recover; short-term triumphs should not induce long-term strategic complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware contagion of foreign political examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The present distemper of France is far more likely to be contagious than the old one: ... in all evils of the opposite kind our natural inclinations are flattered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and guard against the domestic influence of foreign revolutions — especially radical example that flatters popular inclinations — because imitation of destructive innovations can undermine social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer measured reformation over tearing down institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything which unnecessarily tore to pieces the contexture of the state not only prevented all real reformation, but introduced evils which would call, but perhaps call in vain, for new reformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should preserve the 'balances and counterpoises' of a constitution; radical destruction of institutional checks tends to produce greater evils and may preclude successful future reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect property and institutional holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: They laid the axe to the root of all property, and consequently of all national prosperity, by the principles they established and the example they set, in confiscating all the possessions of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation or systematic undermining of property and established institutional holdings (e.g., Church possessions) destroys the foundations of social prosperity and authority, and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abstract declarations that undermine authority
rubrics_metrics.description: They made and recorded ... the Rights of Man, in such a pedantic abuse of elementary principles ... as by their name and authority they systematically destroyed every hold of authority by opinion, religious or civil, on the minds of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights-language and sweeping declarations should be applied with caution; grandiloquent or pedantic pronouncements can erode moral and civil authority if they are used to abolish intermediate institutions that sustain social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clear military discipline and single authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Armies cannot exist under a divided command. ... We have put them under a single authority, with a simple (our common) oath of fidelity; and we keep the whole under our annual inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standing army must be organized under a single, accountable chain of command with clear oaths and periodic civilian oversight; divided or competing military authorities invite disobedience and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate citizen and soldier roles indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: What was done there (France) furnished no matter of exultation, either in the act or the example. These soldiers were not citizens, but base, hireling mutineers ... Their conduct was one of the fruits of that anarchic spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When military forces assume civic political authority or are remade into partisan citizen-armies without discipline, they risk becoming mutinous or instruments of faction rather than a responsible defence force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure responsibility and accountability in military conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: What a dreadful thing is a standing army for the conduct of the whole or any part of which no man is responsible!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every military unit must have responsible commanders (captain, colonel, general) who can be held to account; lack of responsibility in military organization threatens both liberty and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge revolutions by their real effects, not rhetorical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: With them the question was not between despotism and liberty. The sacrifice they made of the peace and power of their country was not made on the altar of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political change by its concrete consequences for social order, property, and national strength rather than by its professed aims or rhetorical claims to liberty.
